patches.new: This property has a consequence that we only preview here. An \emph{eigenvalue} of a square matrix $A$ is a number $\lambda$ for which some nonzero vector $\bm v$ (an \emph{eigenvector}) satisfies $A\bm v=\lambda\bm v$: the matrix merely rescales that vector. Chapter~\ref{ch:eigen} defines these properly and proves that the ``move across the inner product'' property forces the eigenvalues of symmetric and Hermitian matrices to be real. That is why the paper's finite-difference Hamiltonian, a real symmetric matrix (Sec.~II~B), has real energy levels. ``Self-adjoint'' is the name for the same property in operators acting on functions rather than on finite lists, which is why the Hilbert--P\'olya idea (Chapter~\ref{ch:hilbert-polya}) asks for a self-adjoint operator.

patches.old: Dotting with the first row $\bm r_1=(A_{11},A_{12},A_{13})$ reproduces \cref{eq:linear-algebra-det3} term by term (the middle term's sign is absorbed because $A_{23}A_{31}-A_{21}A_{33}=-(A_{21}A_{33}-A_{23}A_{31})$). So $\det A=\bm r_1\cdot(\bm r_2\times\bm r_3)$, and $\abs{\det A}$ is the volume of the parallelepiped spanned by the rows.
By the discussion above (with $\bm b=\bm 0$, which is always consistent), its members are described by $n-r$ free parameters, so it is a subspace of dimension $n-r$.
patches.new: Its size is fixed by the free variables. Take $\bm b=\bm 0$ (always consistent, since $\bm x=\bm 0$ works). For each free variable $i$ ($i=1,\dots,n-r$), set that free variable to $1$ and all other free variables to $0$, and solve for the pivot variables by back substitution; call the result $\bm x^{(i)}$, a \emph{special solution}. (i) The special solutions are independent: in $\sum_i\alpha_i\bm x^{(i)}$ the slot of free variable $i$ contains exactly $\alpha_i$ (only $\bm x^{(i)}$ has a nonzero entry there), so the combination is $\bm 0$ only if every $\alpha_i=0$. (ii) They span the null space: let $A\bm x=\bm 0$ and let $f_i$ be the value of free variable $i$ in $\bm x$. Then $\bm y=\bm x-\sum_if_i\bm x^{(i)}$ satisfies $A\bm y=\bm 0$ and has every free variable equal to $0$; back substitution with zero right side and zero free variables gives every pivot variable $0$, so $\bm y=\bm 0$ and $\bm x=\sum_if_i\bm x^{(i)}$. So the $n-r$ special solutions form a basis of the null space, which is a subspace of dimension $n-r$.

import qmnt

def close(a, b, tol):
    assert abs(a - b) < tol, (a, b)

assert np.allclose(p - d, [-0.5, 0.5, -0.5])

close(np.sqrt(np.mean(r**2)), 0.2739, 1e-4)

close(rmsf(d), 1.5811, 1e-4)
close(np.corrcoef(p, d)[0, 1], 1.0, 1e-12)
close(rmsf(p - d), 0.7906, 1e-4)
close(q @ d, 0.0, 1e-12); close(q @ q, 10.0, 1e-12)
close(rmsf(q - d), 2.2361, 1e-4)
close(rmsf(q - d) / rmsf(d), np.sqrt(2), 1e-12)

# Checkpoint (1,i).(1,i) without conjugate
u = np.array([1, 1j]); close(abs(u @ u), 0.0, 1e-15)

assert np.isclose(np.vdot(v, u), 3 + 1j)
close(np.linalg.norm(u)**2, 6, 1e-12); close(np.linalg.norm(v)**2, 3, 1e-12)
close(abs(np.vdot(u, v))**2, 10, 1e-12)

# Sample: components in rotated basis
e1 = np.array([1, 1]) / np.sqrt(2); e2 = np.array([1, -1]) / np.sqrt(2); vv = np.array([3., 1])

close(a1, 2.8284, 1e-4); close(a2, 1.4142, 1e-4)
assert np.allclose(a1 * e1 + a2 * e2, vv); close(a1**2 + a2**2, 10, 1e-12)

# Sample: projection onto a line

close(a @ (b - pr), 0, 1e-12)

assert np.allclose(g, [6.887315, 3.988818, 5.414018], atol=1e-9)
close(np.diff(t).sum(), 35.639107, 1e-9)

assert np.array_equal(R @ S, [[0, -1], [2, 0]]); assert np.array_equal(S @ R, [[0, -2], [1, 0]])
assert np.array_equal(R @ S @ [1, 0], [0, 2]); assert np.array_equal(S @ R @ [1, 0], [0, 1])

assert np.allclose(np.linalg.solve(A, [1, 2]), [-0.8, 0.6])

# Sample: elimination 3x3, determinant, operation count n=3

close(cost(6000), 7.2e10, 1e7)                     # Problem 27 / text

close(np.linalg.det(Ar), Ar[0] @ np.cross(Ar[1], Ar[2]), 1e-10)

# Pitfall: interior sum of x^2, and trapezoid values
for N, claimed, trap in [(9, 0.48, 0.6800), (99, 0.6468, 0.6668)]:

                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=color, lw=1.8))

ax1.plot([u[0], 4], [u[1], 3], "C1--", lw=0.8)
ax1.plot([v[0], 4], [v[1], 3], "C0--", lw=0.8)

import numpy as np, matplotlib; matplotlib.use("Agg"); import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import qmnt
L = 44.883; nlev = 30; M = 30
n = np.arange(1, nlev+1); k = np.arange(M)
Abox = np.zeros((nlev, M)); Abox[:, 0] = 1
for nn in range(1, nlev+1):
    if nn < M:
        Abox[nn-1, nn] = (-1)**(nn+1)/2
N = 1200
x = qmnt.grid(L, N); h = 2*L/(N+1)
V = np.array([qmnt.wu_sprung_V(xi) for xi in x])
E, vecs = qmnt.fd_levels(V, L, k=nlev, return_vectors=True)
vecs = np.asarray(vecs)
if vecs.shape[0] != N:
    vecs = vecs.T
vecs = vecs[:, :nlev]
vecs = vecs/np.sqrt(h*np.sum(vecs**2, axis=0))
Phi = np.cos(np.outer(x, k)*np.pi/L)
Aws = h*(vecs**2).T @ Phi
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 3))
for ax, Am, ttl in [(ax1, Abox, "infinite well"), (ax2, Aws, "Wu-Sprung")]:
    im = ax.imshow(Am, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-1, vmax=1, origin="upper",
                   extent=[-0.5, M-0.5, nlev+0.5, 0.5])
    ax.set_xlabel("basis index k"); ax.set_title(ttl)
ax1.set_ylabel("level n")
fig.colorbar(im, ax=[ax1, ax2], shrink=0.8, label="A_nk (dimensionless)")
plt.savefig("linear-algebra_Amatrix.pdf", bbox_inches="tight")
